llm_response.content:
Below is a complete empirical plan tailored to your setup. I propose a design that exploits exogenous occupation switches triggered by plant closures and uses the task-based relatedness of occupations (built from BIBB/IAB) to quantify the portability of skills and its impact on wages and occupational choices.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary strategy: Event study with difference-in-differences layered with an instrumental variables approach (event-study-IV).
  - Rationale:
    - Event study/DID: Plant closures are plausibly exogenous to individual productivity and force many workers to change jobs/occupations at a common event time. Comparing wage trajectories of displaced workers who move into more- versus less-related occupations provides credible causal variation in “portability intensity” that affects post-displacement wage dynamics.
    - IV: Even within closure cohorts, more able workers could sort into more-related occupations. I instrument realized destination relatedness using local opportunity-set variation that is predetermined with respect to the individual: (i) a shift-share “relatedness index” based on the initial occupation’s similarity to occupations prevalent in the local labor market at the time of displacement, and/or (ii) leave-one-out peer averages of realized relatedness among other displaced co-workers from the same closure and region. This corrects for sorting and sharpens causal interpretation.
- Secondary strategy: Panel 2SLS for wage decomposition into general, occupation-specific, and portable experience.
  - Estimate a wage equation with worker fixed effects in which the stock of “portable experience” (similarity-weighted past experience relative to the current occupation) is an endogenous regressor. Instrument the increments to this portable stock at job changes using the same opportunity-set instruments at each displacement-driven transition. This provides a structural decomposition of wage growth.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Intensity treatment: Relatedness between the pre-closure occupation o0 and the post-closure destination occupation o1, r = S(o0, o1) ∈ [0,1], where S is a task-based cosine similarity built from BIBB/IAB.
  - For visualization and nonparametric evidence, I will also categorize r into quintiles (Q1=least related, …, Q5=most related).
- Control group:
  - Core: Other displaced workers from plant closures in the same period and region who transition into less-related occupations (e.g., bottom two quintiles of r).
  - For some specifications, I will also include a non-displaced matched group (propensity-score matched on pre-closure occupation, age, tenure, region, plant size) to benchmark overall displacement effects; however, causal inference on portability comes primarily from comparisons within displaced workers by relatedness.
- Treatment timing / event date:
  - Event date τi: the worker’s separation date due to a plant closure. Event time k = t − τi.
- IVs:
  - Local relatedness index (Bartik-style): For worker i with pre-closure occupation o0 in region r at time τ, instrument Z1i = Σk S(o0,k) × share(r, τ, k), where share(r, τ, k) is the employment share of occupation k in the commuting region r in year τ (leave-one-out wrt the closing plant’s workforce).
  - Peer leave-one-out instrument: Z2i = average realized relatedness of other displaced workers from the same closure cohort in the same region (excluding worker i).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- A1. Exogeneity of plant closures: Conditional on plant and time controls, closures are unrelated to workers’ idiosyncratic productivity trends.
  - Plausibility: High in German admin context; closures are typically driven by firm shocks. I will include plant fixed effects in pre-closure outcomes and flexibly control for occupation×year and region×year shocks.
- A2. Parallel pre-trends across relatedness groups: Absent the shock and subsequent occupational assignment, displaced workers who will end up in high- vs low-relatedness occupations would have had similar wage trends pre-closure.
  - Plausibility: Reasonable; to be tested directly via event-time coefficients in the pre-period and by conditioning on rich pre-closure controls (earnings, tenure, occupation).
- A3. IV exclusion: Local occupation composition affects post-displacement wages only through its effect on the relatedness of the destination occupation (and thus portability), not through direct wage-level shocks that differentially hit displaced workers.
  - Plausibility: More demanding. I will include region×year and (pre-closure) occupation×year fixed effects, narrow the window to the first post-closure job within the same region, and use leave-one-out constructions to mitigate mechanical correlations.
- A4. Monotonicity for IV: Higher local relatedness index (or higher peer-relatedness) weakly increases the probability of landing in a more-related occupation.
  - Plausibility: Strong; richer opportunity sets in related occupations should not reduce related moves.
- A5. Stable measurement of S(o,k): BIBB tasks map consistently to the 64 occupations through time, and cosine similarity captures technological/task proximity.
  - Plausibility: High given standardized German occupations and repeated BIBB; I will verify robustness to alternative similarity measures and decades.

4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
- T1. Selection even among displaced: High-ability workers might systematically find more-related destinations (higher r), biasing estimates upward.
  - Remedies:
    - Instrument r using Z1 (local relatedness index) and Z2 (peer leave-one-out).
    - Rich controls: pre-closure wage level and growth, tenure, education, plant size, pre-closure occupation, and worker FE in panel decompositions.
    - Restrict to first job within 6 months and within the same commuting region to minimize endogenous search/migration.
- T2. Direct demand shocks in related occupations: The local composition that makes related moves feasible may also raise wages directly, violating exclusion.
  - Remedies:
    - Include region×year and occupation×year fixed effects.
    - Use leave-one-out construction that removes the closing plant’s workforce and, in robustness, subtract the contribution of the destination firm.
    - Event-study focus: compare across relatedness bins within the same closure cohort and region-time where feasible.
- T3. Wage right-censoring at the social security ceiling:
  - Remedies:
    - Baseline: drop censored observations or Winsorize at the cap, and re-estimate on uncensored subsample.
    - Robustness: impute using Pareto tail methods or estimate with censored FE Tobit; also show results using median regressions below the cap.
- Additional concerns and mitigations:
  - Measurement error in S(o,k): Try multiple definitions (cosine on all tasks, cosine on top 5 tasks, main-task match indicator) and decade-specific S matrices.
  - Anticipation/early moves: Exclude moves >6 months pre-closure; verify no pre-trends in occupational switching or wages.

5. R Code Outline
Note: Illustrative, assumes CSVs exist and keys align. Uses fixest for high-dimensional FE and IV.

Libraries and data loading
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(Matrix)
library(stringr)

# Load data
admin <- fread("admin_spells.csv")          # worker_id, plant_id, occ2d, start_date, end_date, daily_wage, region_id, education, birth_year
bibb  <- fread("bibb_tasks.csv")            # occ2d, wave_year, task_id (1..19), task_share
occ_shares <- fread("region_occ_shares.csv")# region_id, year, occ2d, emp_share
cpi <- fread("cpi_deflator.csv")            # year, cpi

# Preprocess dates and wages
admin[, start := as.IDate(start_date)]
admin[, end   := as.IDate(end_date)]
admin[, year  := year(start)]
admin <- merge(admin, cpi, by="year", all.x=TRUE)
admin[, ln_w := log(daily_wage / cpi)]

Step 1: Build occupation similarity matrix S from BIBB
# Average task shares by occ across waves to smooth
bibb_occ <- bibb[, .(task_share = mean(task_share, na.rm=TRUE)), by=.(occ2d, task_id)]
# Wide matrix occ x task
bibb_wide <- dcast(bibb_occ, occ2d ~ task_id, value.var="task_share", fill=0)
occ_codes <- bibb_wide$occ2d
V <- as.matrix(bibb_wide[, -1])
# Normalize rows
row_norm <- function(M) M / sqrt(rowSums(M^2) + 1e-12)
Vn <- row_norm(V)
# Cosine similarity S = Vn %*% t(Vn)
S <- Vn %*% t(Vn)
rownames(S) <- occ_codes
colnames(S) <- occ_codes

# Helper: get similarity between two occupations
get_sim <- function(o_from, o_to) {
  if (!o_from %in% rownames(S) | !o_to %in% colnames(S)) return(NA_real_)
  as.numeric(S[o_from, o_to])
}

Step 2: Identify plant closures
# Define a closure if plant disappears and >=80% of workers separate within 90 days
setkey(admin, plant_id, start, end)
# Identify last appearance of plant
plant_last_end <- admin[, .(last_end = max(end, na.rm=TRUE)), by=plant_id]
# Workers leaving near last_end
admin <- merge(admin, plant_last_end, by="plant_id", all.x=TRUE)
admin[, close_sep := as.integer(abs(as.numeric(end - last_end)) <= 90)]
# Closure size metric
closure_flag <- admin[close_sep==1, .(sep_count = .N,
                                      uniq_workers = uniqueN(worker_id)),
                      by=.(plant_id, last_end)]
closure_flag[, share_sep := sep_count / uniq_workers]
closures <- closure_flag[share_sep >= 0.8][, .(plant_id, closure_date=last_end)]
# Tag closure separations
admin <- merge(admin, closures, by="plant_id", all.x=TRUE)
admin[, displaced := as.integer(!is.na(closure_date) & close_sep==1)]

Step 3: Build displacement cohort and first destination occupation with relatedness
# Pre-closure occupation: occupation in the job that ends at closure_date
pre <- admin[displaced==1, .SD[.N], by=.(worker_id, plant_id, closure_date)][
  , .(worker_id, region_id, closure_date, pre_occ = occ2d, pre_ln_w = ln_w, pre_year = year, pre_tenure_days = as.integer(end - start) + 1)]

# Post-closure first job within 6 months and same region
post <- admin[, .(next_start = start, next_occ=occ2d, next_ln_w=ln_w, next_region=region_id, next_year=year),
              by=.(worker_id)]
# Merge and restrict
cohort <- merge(pre, post, by="worker_id", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
cohort <- cohort[next_start > closure_date & next_start <= closure_date + 183]
cohort <- cohort[region_id == next_region]  # stay in region to reduce endogenous migration
# Keep earliest next job
setorder(cohort, worker_id, next_start)
cohort <- cohort[, .SD[1], by=worker_id]

# Compute relatedness r = S(pre_occ, next_occ)
cohort[, relatedness := mapply(get_sim, pre_occ, next_occ)]
cohort <- cohort[!is.na(relatedness)]

# Event-time panel around closure (e.g., -3..+5 years)
# Build annual panel of wages for displaced around τ with worker and calendar-year info
w_panel <- admin[worker_id %in% cohort$worker_id]
w_panel <- merge(w_panel, cohort[, .(worker_id, closure_date, pre_occ, relatedness)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)
w_panel <- w_panel[!is.na(closure_date)]
w_panel[, event_year := year - year(closure_date)]
w_panel <- w_panel[event_year >= -3 & event_year <= 5]
# Create event-time dummies excluding -1 as baseline
for (k in c(-3,-2,0,1,2,3,4,5)) w_panel[, paste0("E",k) := as.integer(event_year==k)]

Step 4: Instruments for relatedness
# 4.1 Local relatedness index Z1 at time of displacement
# Merge region-occ shares at closure year
cohort[, closure_year := year(closure_date)]
tmp <- merge(occ_shares, cohort[, .(worker_id, region_id, closure_year, pre_occ)], 
             by.x=c("region_id","year"), by.y=c("region_id","closure_year"), all.y=TRUE)

# For each worker, compute Z1 = sum_k S(pre_occ,k)*share(r,year,k)
# Precompute S rows as data.table
S_dt <- as.data.table(as.table(S))
setnames(S_dt, c("Var1","Var2","N"), c("pre_occ","occ2d","sim"))

tmp <- merge(tmp, S_dt, by=c("pre_occ","occ2d"), all.x=TRUE)
tmp[is.na(sim), sim := 0]
Z1 <- tmp[, .(Z1 = sum(sim * emp_share, na.rm=TRUE)), by=.(worker_id)]
cohort <- merge(cohort, Z1, by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)

# 4.2 Peer leave-one-out Z2: average relatedness of other displaced from same plant&closure year&region
cohort[, closure_key := paste(plant_id, closure_year, region_id, sep="_")]
# Merge plant_id into cohort
cohort <- merge(cohort, pre[, .(worker_id, plant_id)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)
cohort[, closure_key := paste(plant_id, closure_year, region_id, sep="_")]
peer <- cohort[, .(peer_mean = (sum(relatedness) - relatedness) / pmax(.N-1,1)), by=.(closure_key, worker_id)]
cohort <- merge(cohort, peer[, .(worker_id, Z2=peer_mean)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)

# Attach instruments back to event-time panel
w_panel <- merge(w_panel, cohort[, .(worker_id, relatedness, Z1, Z2)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)

Step 5: Event-study-IV: effect of relatedness on wage dynamics post-closure
# Interact event-time dummies with instrumented relatedness (constant per event)
# First, build interaction regressors for post periods (exclude -1, use k = 0..5)
post_ks <- c(0,1,2,3,4,5)
for (k in post_ks) {
  w_panel[, paste0("R_E",k) := get(paste0("E",k)) * relatedness]
  w_panel[, paste0("Z1_E",k) := get(paste0("E",k)) * Z1]
  w_panel[, paste0("Z2_E",k) := get(paste0("E",k)) * Z2]
}

# Baseline controls
w_panel[, age := (year - birth_year)]
w_panel[, pretrend_lnw := mean(ln_w[event_year %in% -3:-1], na.rm=TRUE), by=worker_id]

# IV event study: ln_w_it = sum_k beta_k * (E_k * relatedness_hat) + worker FE + calendar-year FE + occ(pre)×year FE + region×year FE + X
iv_rhs <- paste(paste0("R_E", post_ks), collapse=" + ")
iv_z1  <- paste(paste0("Z1_E", post_ks), collapse=" + ")
iv_z2  <- paste(paste0("Z2_E", post_ks), collapse=" + ")

# Use Z1 as main IV; can stack Z1 & Z2 for over-ID
fml_iv <- as.formula(paste0("ln_w ~ ", 
                            # include pre-period event dummies (not interacted) to check pre-trends if desired
                            paste(paste0("E", c(-3,-2,0,1,2,3,4,5)), collapse=" + "),
                            " | worker_id + year + pre_occ^year + region_id^year | ",
                            iv_rhs, " ~ ", iv_z1))

est_es <- feols(fml_iv, data=w_panel[!is.na(ln_w) & !is.na(relatedness)],
                cluster = ~ plant_id)  # cluster at plant (closure) level if plant_id merged

summary(est_es)

# Graph implied beta_k (coefficients on R_Ek) to visualize how higher relatedness shifts wage path after closure

Robustness 1: Use peer IV Z2 (or both IVs)
fml_iv2 <- as.formula(paste0("ln_w ~ ", paste(paste0("E", c(-3,-2,0,1,2,3,4,5)), collapse=" + "),
                             " | worker_id + year + pre_occ^year + region_id^year | ",
                             iv_rhs, " ~ ", iv_z2))
est_es2 <- feols(fml_iv2, data=w_panel[!is.na(ln_w) & !is.na(relatedness)], cluster = ~ plant_id)
summary(est_es2)

Robustness 2: Drop top-coded wages
# Suppose admin has indicator top_censored (1 if at cap)
est_es_nc <- feols(fml_iv, data=w_panel[top_censored==0], cluster = ~ plant_id)
summary(est_es_nc)

Step 6: Wage growth decomposition via portable experience
# Construct experience stocks:
# GE_it: total years since first job
# OSE_it: cumulative years in current occ2d
# PE_it: sum over past occupations k != current o of S(o,k) * years in k

# First, order spells per worker
setorder(admin, worker_id, start)
# Compute cumulative general experience in years
admin[, ge_years := as.numeric(cumsum((as.numeric(end - start) + 1)/365)), by=worker_id]

# Occupation-specific and portable experience
admin[, occ_change := shift(occ2d, type="lag") != occ2d, by=worker_id]
admin[, cum_ose := 0.0]
admin[, cum_pe  := 0.0]

# For simplicity, compute at spell-level using past history
admin[, `:=`(cum_ose = 0, cum_pe = 0)]
admin[, curr_occ := occ2d]

# Build past history table to compute PE at each spell start
build_PE <- function(dt) {
  dt <- copy(dt)
  dt[, cum_ose := 0.0]
  dt[, cum_pe  := 0.0]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(dt))) {
    if (i==1) next
    curr <- dt$occ2d[i]
    past <- dt[1:(i-1)]
    # OSE: time spent previously in current occ
    ose <- sum((as.numeric(past$end - past$start) + 1)/365 * as.integer(past$occ2d == curr))
    # PE: sum over past occs weighted by similarity to current
    pe  <- sum(((as.numeric(past$end - past$start) + 1)/365) * sapply(past$occ2d, function(k) get_sim(curr, k)) * as.integer(past$occ2d != curr), na.rm=TRUE)
    dt$cum_ose[i] <- ose
    dt$cum_pe[i]  <- pe
  }
  dt
}
admin_pe <- admin[, build_PE(.SD), by=worker_id]

# Merge instruments for increments to PE at displacement-driven switches
# Define indicator if spell started after closure for that worker
admin_pe <- merge(admin_pe, pre[, .(worker_id, closure_date)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)
admin_pe[, after_closure := as.integer(!is.na(closure_date) & start > closure_date)]
# Compute instrumented increment: at spells that start after closure, use RI (Z1) at closure and multiply by years in new spell so far
admin_pe <- merge(admin_pe, cohort[, .(worker_id, Z1)], by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)
admin_pe[, inc_pe_iv := ifelse(after_closure==1, Z1 * as.numeric((end - start) + 1)/365, 0)]
# Cumulative IV for PE is sum of inc_pe_iv up to current spell
admin_pe[, cum_pe_iv := cumsum(inc_pe_iv), by=worker_id]

# Panel wage equation with worker FE, instrument cum_pe by cum_pe_iv
# Controls: ge_years, cum_ose; FE: worker + occ2d×year + region×year
decomp <- feols(ln_w ~ ge_years + cum_ose + fregion = i(region_id, year) + focc = i(occ2d, year) | worker_id,
                iv = ~ cum_pe ~ cum_pe_iv,
                data = admin_pe[top_censored==0], cluster = ~ worker_id)
summary(decomp)

# Compute contribution shares: use estimated betas to decompose predicted wage growth between 5 and 15 years of experience
# (Post-estimation calculation not shown here)

6. Expected Results
- Direction:
  - Event-study: Higher relatedness (more portable skills) should mitigate wage losses at displacement and accelerate wage recovery; beta_k > 0 for post periods, with strongest effects 1–3 years after closure.
  - Wage decomposition: All three components—general, occupation-specific, and portable—should have positive returns. Portable experience should matter materially when workers land in related occupations.
- Magnitude (priors from human capital theory and international evidence):
  - Returns per year:
    - General experience: ~2% per year early in career, flattening later.
    - Occupation-specific: ~1–1.5% per year within the current occupation.
    - Portable (similarity-weighted) experience: ~1–2% per “similarity-weighted” year when S ≈ 0.5–1.0 (so 0.5–1.0% for moderately related past experience). Aggregated across careers with early related switches, portable experience could explain 25–40% of cumulative wage growth from ages ~20 to 40.
  - Event-study: Moving to a top-quintile related occupation vs bottom quintile likely reduces immediate wage loss by 3–6 pp and increases 3-year post-displacement wages by 5–10 pp.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Exogenous shock (plant closure) plausibly unrelated to individual trends after controls: 1
- C2: Parallel pre-trends across relatedness groups verified in event time: 1
- C3: Strong first stage for IV (local relatedness and peer IV predict realized relatedness): 1
- C4: Exclusion restriction for IV (local composition affects wages only via relatedness), after rich FE: 0
- C5: No differential selective attrition around event (employment/wage observation probabilities): 0

Notes and implementation details
- Occupation similarity robustness: Recompute S using (i) cosine on all 19 tasks, (ii) cosine on top-5 tasks per occupation, (iii) main-task match indicator; re-estimate.
- Commuting regions: Use standardized German Raumordnungsregionen if available to define region_id.
- Plant closures: Sensitivity to alternative thresholds (e.g., 70–90% separations; 60–120 day windows) and to excluding multi-plant conglomerates where reallocation may blur closures.
- Censoring: Report results on uncensored sample, Tobit FE, and imputed top codes.
- Standard errors: Cluster at closure cohort (plant×closure year) for event-study; at worker for panel decomposition; add two-way clustering (closure, region-year) in robustness.
